# Board approves new name for UIC Law

May 20, 2021

[![Image 7: UIC School of Law logo](https://today.uic.edu/wp-content/uploads/2021/05/COL.LAW_.LOCKB_.SM_.RGB_.JPG-750wide-390x164.jpg)](https://today.uic.edu/uic_law_informal_lockup-logo-full-color-rgb_uic_law_informal_loc [link_23])

The UIC John Marshall Law School will change its name to the University of Illinois Chicago School of Law after receiving approval from the University of Illinois Board of Trustees today.

With all required approvals and agreements obtained in accordance with university processes and contractual obligations with the Legacy Law School Corporation and the Foundation Legacy Corporation (the successor legal entities that owned and operated the law school, and fund-raised for the school, before it became a part of UIC), the name change will be effective July 1, 2021.

The vote comes after months of review by a task force that gathered input from students, faculty, staff, and alumni, conducted research and proposed principles to guide the institution in evaluating a potential name change.

The task force report noted, “that despite Chief Justice Marshall’s legacy as one of the nation’s most significant U.S. Supreme Court justices, the newly discovered research regarding his role as a slave trader, slave owner of hundreds of slaves, pro-slavery jurisprudence, and racist views render him a highly inappropriate namesake for the Law School.”

“The university has arrived at this new name following a thorough and carefully studied process that included input from all corners of the institution and beyond, considered issues of racial injustice and aimed to ensure that our university continues to be a place where diversity, inclusion and equal opportunity are supported and advanced,” said UIC Chancellor Michael Amiridis.

Following the task force’s report in February and its 6-1 membership recommendation to rename the school, law school faculty voted in favor of a new official name in March. Approval from the Legacy Law School Corporation and the Foundation Legacy Corporation was received last week by the University of Illinois System.

The John Marshall Law School, formerly an independent law school that was established in 1899, merged with UIC in 2019 to create UIC John Marshall Law School. Since its founding, the school has upheld a tradition of diversity, innovation and opportunity and consistently provided an education that combined an understanding of the theory, philosophy and practice of law.

“The name of the school has changed, but it doesn’t erase its proud history or the impact of its faculty, alumni and students. As Chicago’s first and only public law school, our mission continues to center on academic excellence, diversity, student success and bettering the lives of the people of Chicago and beyond,” said Darby Dickerson, dean of the Law School.

To learn more about the University of Illinois Chicago School of Law, which is based at Jackson and State streets in the heart of the Loop and the city’s legal district, visit [go.uic.edu/uiclaw](link_24).

The **University of Illinois Chicago School of Law** (**UIC Law**) is the [law school](link_8) of the [University of Illinois Chicago](link_0), a [public](link_7)[research university](link_16) in [Chicago](link_10), Illinois. Founded in 1899, it became affiliated with the university in 2019. The school offers programs for both part-time and full-time students, with both day and night classes available, and offers January enrollment.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

UIC Law was founded in 1899 as the **John Marshall Law School** and initially accredited by the [American Bar Association](link_14) in 1951. It merged with the [University of Illinois at Chicago](link_17) in 2019, becoming the University of Illinois Chicago John Marshall Law School.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law#cite_note-4) On May 20, 2021, following review by a university task force, the school announced its official change of name to University of Illinois Chicago School of Law, effective July 1.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law#cite_note-5) The board of trustees acknowledged that "newly discovered research",[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law#cite_note-ChicagoS-T-6) uncovered by historian [Paul Finkelman](link_18),[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law#cite_note-7) had revealed that influential 19th century [U.S. Supreme Court](link_19) chief justice [John Marshall](link_20) was a slave trader and owner who practiced "pro-slavery jurisprudence", which was deemed inappropriate for the school's namesake.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law#cite_note-ChicagoS-T-6)

UIC Law is located in Chicago's central financial and legal district, most commonly known as [The Loop](link_21). It is across the street from the [Dirksen Federal Building](link_22), which houses the [U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit](link_23) and the [U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Illinois](link_24), and about four blocks from the [Daley Center](link_25), which houses the [Circuit Court of Cook County](link_26) and the Bilandic Building site of the [Illinois Appellate Court](link_27) (First District). The [Chicago Bar Association](link_28) is next door to the law school.

## Admissions and costs

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Admissions and costs")]

For the class entering in 2023, UIC Law accepted 69.53% of applicants, with 27.96% of those accepted enrolling. The average enrollee had a 152 [LSAT](link_29) score and 3.39 undergraduate [GPA](link_30).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law#cite_note-Standard_509-1) Tuition and fees at UIC Law for the 2020-2021 academic year is $39,014 for Illinois residents and $48,014 for out of state residents.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law#cite_note-8)

## Academics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Academics")]

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c5/John_Marshall_Law.jpg/250px-John_Marshall_Law.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:John_Marshall_Law.jpg)

The former name, John Marshall Law School

### Curriculum

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Curriculum")]

UIC Law has day and evening divisions, with identical instruction, course content, and scholastic requirements. Lawyering Skills courses, which focus on writing, research, and oral argument, are an integral part of the core curriculum. These courses are taught in small groups, to maximize the individual attention given to each student. A student may earn a J.D. certificate in a certain area of the law or focus more emphatically and earn a joint degree (J.D./LL.M.).

The law school also offers Master of Laws (LL.M.) and Master of Jurisprudence (M.J.) programs for practicing attorneys and non-attorney professionals and other individual students.

UIC School of Law offers seven [Master of Laws](link_31) (LL.M.) programs for attorneys seeking specialized education in legal issues and for current J.D. students who would like the maximum concentration in particular areas of the law. UIC Law offers a comprehensive curriculum in the following areas: Employee Benefits Law, Estate Planning, Information Technology and [Privacy Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Privacy_Law "Privacy Law"), Intellectual Property Law, International Business and Trade Law, [Real Estate Law](link_32), and Tax Law.

### Journals and organizations

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Journals and organizations")]

There are four honors programs: _UIC Law Review_, _[UIC Review of Intellectual Property Law](link_33)_ ("RIPL"), the [Moot Court](link_34) Honors Program, and the Trial Advocacy & Dispute Resolution Honors Program.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law#cite_note-9) UIC Law sends teams to more than 30 moot court and mock trial competitions annually.

University of Illinois trustees voted to remove the name of the longest-serving U.S. Supreme Court chief justice from the University of Illinois-Chicago law school after a task force said John Marshall’s history as a slave owner and trader “render him a highly inappropriate namesake for the law school.”

The University of Illinois at Chicago merged with the private John Marshall Law School in 2019 to create the city’s first public law school, named UIC John Marshall Law School. It will be renamed the UI-Chicago School of Law effective July 1, the News-Gazette reported.

The trustees’ vote Thursday followed a months-long review by a university task force, which voted 6-1 to remove Marshall’s name. The law school faculty and faculty senate also voted in favor of renaming the school, which is separate from the University of Illinois College of Law in Urbana.

The task force report issued in February stated that despite Marshall’s legacy “as one of the nation’s most significant U.S. Supreme Court justices, the newly discovered research regarding his role as a slave trader, slave owner of hundreds of slaves, pro-slavery jurisprudence, and racist views render him a highly inappropriate namesake for the law school.”

In a statement, UIC Chancellor Michael Amiridis said the name change followed a “thorough and carefully studied process” with input from inside and outside the institution and “considered issues of racial injustice and aimed to ensure that our university continues to be a place where diversity, inclusion and equal opportunity are supported and advanced,” the Chicago Sun-Times reported.

John Marshall Law School was established in 1899. As part of the 2019 merger, the University of Illinois agreed to keep the phrase “John Marshall Law School” in the name for at least five years. Thursday’s vote was needed to amend the transfer agreement and allow for the name change to take effect this year.

## University of Illinois - Cookie Information

### About Cookies

Cookies and related technologies (herein “Cookies”) are small text files that a website saves on your computer when you visit the site. Cookies the University sets are called first-party Cookies. The data collected might be about you, your device, your preferences, or your login information. This data is mostly used to make the website work as expected so, for example, you don’t have to keep re-entering your credentials whenever you come back to the site. Cookies set by third parties are called third-party Cookies. We use third-party Cookies for analyzing website traffic and our advertising and marketing efforts. We have divided the Cookies we use into the following categories: Strictly Necessary, Performance, Functional, and Targeting. Under each category heading below you will find a general description of the Cookies in each category. You can change your browser settings to block, delete, or alert you to Cookies. The Help menu on the menu bar of most browsers will tell you how to do that. However, if you do, you may have to manually adjust preferences every time you visit a site and some features may not work as intended.

See the [**University of Illinois System Cookie Policy**Link opens in a new window](https://www.vpaa.uillinois.edu/resources/cookies) for more information.

 Strictly Necessary Cookies - Always Active 
Strictly Necessary Cookies are first-party Cookies that are necessary for the website to function. They can be either permanent or temporary and are usually only set in response to actions made directly by you that amount to a request for services, such as logging in or filling in forms. For example, we use Strictly Necessary Cookies to handle user registration and login. Some sites require the use of Strictly Necessary Cookies to access the site, such as University websites requiring University credentialed authentication. If you set your browser to block or delete Cookies, you may not be able to access the site or some parts of the site will not work.

 Performance Cookies - Always Active 
Performance Cookies allow us to count visits and traffic sources so we can measure and improve the performance and effectiveness of University websites. Performance Cookies also help the University understand which webpages are the most and least popular, see how visitors move around the site, and determine whether webpage content is relevant to user interests. Performance Cookies may be first-party or third party, permanent or temporary, and do not personally identify individual visitors. Some Performance Cookies are “analytics” Cookies (e.g., Google Analytics), using third-party software tools, which help us understand more about how our websites are used and where visitors come from by collecting and aggregating anonymous information on the pages visited and any advertisements viewed. The University does not take responsibility for the collection, use, and management of data by any third-party software tool provider unless required to do so by applicable law. If you set your browser to block or delete Cookies, some site services and functionalities may not work.

 Functional Cookies - Always Active 
Functional Cookies enhance the performance and functionality of our websites but are non-essential to their use. These permanent Cookies allow our website to remember information from your previous visits, such as details you submitted before or your previously stated preferences. These Cookies may also be used to provide services you request, such as newsletters or publications. They may be first- or third-party Cookies that enable services we have added to our webpages. If you set your browser to block or delete Cookies, some or all of these services may not function properly.

 Targeting Cookies - Always Active 
Targeting Cookies are used to deliver content tailored to your interests and may be temporary or permanent. They may also be first-party or third-party Cookies. Targeting Cookies are based on uniquely identifying your browser and device; they do not store information such as your name. The University may use targeting Cookies prepared by the University, its third-party contractors, or advertising partners to provide you with personalized University display advertising and promotional material about the University and its programs. The University may also allow third parties to place Cookies on your device that collect and use anonymous information about your visits to, and interactions with, our websites to personalize advertisements and promotional materials for University goods and services. Targeting Cookies may be used by our third-party contractors or our advertising partners to build a profile of your interests and show you relevant advertisements on other sites. We may share information about your use of our site with our social media, advertising, and analytics partners who may combine it with other information that you have provided to them or that they have collected from your use of their services. If you set your browser to block or delete Cookies, you will still see advertisements, but they will be less targeted to your interests.

**Our efforts to provide access to more students across the state are producing results, including increasing the number of underrepresented students.** In the fall of 2025, underrepresented students made up 33 percent of all undergraduate students in the U of I System, an all-time high.

[EXPLORE ENROLLMENT DATA](link_42)

## EXTRAORDINARY REACH

**From Rockford to Chicago to the Quad Cities, Peoria and the southern tip of Illinois, the University of Illinois System touches virtually every field, forest and city block in our state.** In fact, more than half of all students enrolled in a public university in Illinois are enrolled at one of our three universities. We have students from 101 of 102 Illinois counties, and 79 percent of our undergraduates are in-state students.

**Our commitment to access provides the opportunity to obtain a life-changing education to more students than ever.** To make that possible, nearly half the aid our undergraduate students received – $298 million in Fiscal Year 2024 – comes from our universities. ## University of Illinois - Cookie Information

### About Cookies

Cookies and related technologies (herein “Cookies”) are small text files that a website saves on your computer when you visit the site. Cookies the University sets are called first-party Cookies. The data collected might be about you, your device, your preferences, or your login information. This data is mostly used to make the website work as expected so, for example, you don’t have to keep re-entering your credentials whenever you come back to the site. Cookies set by third parties are called third-party Cookies. We use third-party Cookies for analyzing website traffic and our advertising and marketing efforts. We have divided the Cookies we use into the following categories: Strictly Necessary, Performance, Functional, and Targeting. Under each category heading below you will find a general description of the Cookies in each category. You can change your browser settings to block, delete, or alert you to Cookies. The Help menu on the menu bar of most browsers will tell you how to do that. However, if you do, you may have to manually adjust preferences every time you visit a site and some features may not work as intended.

See the [**University of Illinois System Cookie Policy**Link opens in a new window](https://www.vpaa.uillinois.edu/resources/cookies) for more information.

 Strictly Necessary Cookies - Always Active 
Strictly Necessary Cookies are first-party Cookies that are necessary for the website to function. They can be either permanent or temporary and are usually only set in response to actions made directly by you that amount to a request for services, such as logging in or filling in forms. For example, we use Strictly Necessary Cookies to handle user registration and login. Some sites require the use of Strictly Necessary Cookies to access the site, such as University websites requiring University credentialed authentication. If you set your browser to block or delete Cookies, you may not be able to access the site or some parts of the site will not work.

 Performance Cookies - Always Active 
Performance Cookies allow us to count visits and traffic sources so we can measure and improve the performance and effectiveness of University websites. Performance Cookies also help the University understand which webpages are the most and least popular, see how visitors move around the site, and determine whether webpage content is relevant to user interests. Performance Cookies may be first-party or third party, permanent or temporary, and do not personally identify individual visitors. Some Performance Cookies are “analytics” Cookies (e.g., Google Analytics), using third-party software tools, which help us understand more about how our websites are used and where visitors come from by collecting and aggregating anonymous information on the pages visited and any advertisements viewed. The University does not take responsibility for the collection, use, and management of data by any third-party software tool provider unless required to do so by applicable law. If you set your browser to block or delete Cookies, some site services and functionalities may not work.

 Functional Cookies - Always Active 
Functional Cookies enhance the performance and functionality of our websites but are non-essential to their use. These permanent Cookies allow our website to remember information from your previous visits, such as details you submitted before or your previously stated preferences. These Cookies may also be used to provide services you request, such as newsletters or publications. They may be first- or third-party Cookies that enable services we have added to our webpages. If you set your browser to block or delete Cookies, some or all of these services may not function properly.

 Targeting Cookies - Always Active 
Targeting Cookies are used to deliver content tailored to your interests and may be temporary or permanent. They may also be first-party or third-party Cookies. Targeting Cookies are based on uniquely identifying your browser and device; they do not store information such as your name. # Indiana University Robert H. McKinney School of Law

*   [![Image 3](https://www.theindianalawyer.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/SportsLaw_Lach_Julie_100825-1024x690.jpg)](https://www.theindianalawyer.com/articles/new-iu-indy-program-to-blend-sports-management-with-training-on-foundational-legal-principles [link_81]) ## [New IU Indy program to blend sports management and law](link_81)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

University committed to research as a central part of its mission

[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d8/Sir_Thomas_Lawrence_%281769-1830%29_-_Charles_William%2C_Baron_von_Humboldt_%281767-1835%29_-_RCIN_404936_-_Royal_Collection.jpg/250px-Sir_Thomas_Lawrence_%281769-1830%29_-_Charles_William%2C_Baron_von_Humboldt_%281767-1835%29_-_RCIN_404936_-_Royal_Collection.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sir_Thomas_Lawrence_(1769-1830)_-_Charles_William,_Baron_von_Humboldt_(1767-1835)_-_RCIN_404936_-_Royal_Collection.jpg)

[Wilhelm von Humboldt](link_3), credited with the [Humboldtian model of higher education](link_4)

A **research university** or a **research-intensive university** is a [university](link_5) that is committed to [research](link_0) as a central part of its mission.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-Role-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-Altbach-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-Taylor-4) They are "the key sites of [knowledge production](link_6)", along with "intergenerational [knowledge transfer](link_7) and the certification of new knowledge" through the awarding of [doctoral degrees](link_8), and continue to be "the very center of scientific productivity".[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-Powell-5) They can be [public](link_9) or [private](link_10), and often have well-known brand names.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-CollegeSolution-6)

Undergraduate courses at many research universities are often academic rather than [vocational](link_11) and may not prepare students for particular careers, but many employers value degrees from research universities because they teach fundamental [life skills](link_12) such as [critical thinking](link_13).[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-Andreatta2-7) Globally, research universities are overwhelmingly [public institutions](link_14), while some countries like the United States and Japan also have well-known [private](link_15) research institutions.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-Role-1)

Institutions of higher education that are not research universities or do not aspire to that designation, such as [liberal arts colleges](link_16), instead place more emphasis on student instruction or other aspects of tertiary education, whereas research university faculty members, in contrast, are under more pressure to [publish or perish](link_17).[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-Irons-8)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Research_university&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

### 19th century

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Research_university&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: 19th century")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6e/Interior_of_the_Hutzler_Reading_room_located_in_Gilman_Hall%2C_on_the_Johns_Hopkins_University_campus_in_Baltimore%2C_Maryland_LCCN2013646484.tif/lossy-page1-250px-Interior_of_the_Hutzler_Reading_room_located_in_Gilman_Hall%2C_on_the_Johns_Hopkins_University_campus_in_Baltimore%2C_Maryland_LCCN2013646484.tif.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Interior_of_the_Hutzler_Reading_room_located_in_Gilman_Hall,_on_the_Johns_Hopkins_University_campus_in_Baltimore,_Maryland_LCCN2013646484.tif)

[Johns Hopkins University](link_18) in [Baltimore, Maryland](link_19) (Gilman Hall pictured), founded in 1876, is considered the first research university in the [United States](link_20)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-Geiger_Page_8-9)

The concept of the research university first arose in early 19th-century [Prussia](link_21) in Germany, where [Wilhelm von Humboldt](link_3) championed his vision of _Einheit von Lehre und Forschung_ (the unity of teaching and research), as a means of producing an education that focused on the main areas of knowledge, including the natural sciences, social sciences, and [humanities](link_22), rather than on the previous goals of the university education, which was to develop an understanding of truth, beauty, and [goodness](link_23).[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-Menand-11)

The concept was brought to Britain in the mid-19th century by [Henry Enfield Roscoe](link_24), who had studied with [Robert Wilhelm Bunsen](link_25) at the [University of Heidelberg](link_26). In 1857 he was appointed professor of chemistry at [Owen's College, Manchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Owen [link_27]'s_College,_Manchester "Owen's College, Manchester"), and worked during the 1860s to develop the college following the [German model](link_4).[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-15) The emphasis on research from the German model was taken up by the other

## University of Illinois - Cookie Information

### About Cookies

Cookies and related technologies (herein “Cookies”) are small text files that a website saves on your computer when you visit the site. Cookies the University sets are called first-party Cookies. The data collected might be about you, your device, your preferences, or your login information. This data is mostly used to make the website work as expected so, for example, you don’t have to keep re-entering your credentials whenever you come back to the site. Cookies set by third parties are called third-party Cookies. We use third-party Cookies for analyzing website traffic and our advertising and marketing efforts. We have divided the Cookies we use into the following categories: Strictly Necessary, Performance, Functional, and Targeting. Under each category heading below you will find a general description of the Cookies in each category. You can change your browser settings to block, delete, or alert you to Cookies. The Help menu on the menu bar of most browsers will tell you how to do that. However, if you do, you may have to manually adjust preferences every time you visit a site and some features may not work as intended.

See the [**University of Illinois System Cookie Policy**Link opens in a new window](https://www.vpaa.uillinois.edu/resources/cookies) for more information.

 Strictly Necessary Cookies - Always Active 
Strictly Necessary Cookies are first-party Cookies that are necessary for the website to function. They can be either permanent or temporary and are usually only set in response to actions made directly by you that amount to a request for services, such as logging in or filling in forms. For example, we use Strictly Necessary Cookies to handle user registration and login. Some sites require the use of Strictly Necessary Cookies to access the site, such as University websites requiring University credentialed authentication. If you set your browser to block or delete Cookies, you may not be able to access the site or some parts of the site will not work.

 Performance Cookies - Always Active 
Performance Cookies allow us to count visits and traffic sources so we can measure and improve the performance and effectiveness of University websites. Performance Cookies also help the University understand which webpages are the most and least popular, see how visitors move around the site, and determine whether webpage content is relevant to user interests. Performance Cookies may be first-party or third party, permanent or temporary, and do not personally identify individual visitors. Some Performance Cookies are “analytics” Cookies (e.g., Google Analytics), using third-party software tools, which help us understand more about how our websites are used and where visitors come from by collecting and aggregating anonymous information on the pages visited and any advertisements viewed. The University does not take responsibility for the collection, use, and management of data by any third-party software tool provider unless required to do so by applicable law. If you set your browser to block or delete Cookies, some site services and functionalities may not work.

 Functional Cookies - Always Active 
Functional Cookies enhance the performance and functionality of our websites but are non-essential to their use. These permanent Cookies allow our website to remember information from your previous visits, such as details you submitted before or your previously stated preferences. These Cookies may also be used to provide services you request, such as newsletters or publications. They may be first- or third-party Cookies that enable services we have added to our webpages. If you set your browser to block or delete Cookies, some or all of these services may not function properly.

 Targeting Cookies - Always Active 
Targeting Cookies are used to deliver content tailored to your interests and may be temporary or permanent. They may also be first-party or third-party Cookies. Targeting Cookies are based on uniquely identifying your browser and device; they do not store information such as your name. The University may use targeting Cookies prepared by the University, its third-party contractors, or advertising partners to provide you with personalized University display advertising and promotional material about the University and its programs. The University may also allow third parties to place Cookies on your device that collect and use anonymous information about your visits to, and interactions with, our websites to personalize advertisements and promotional materials for University goods and services. Targeting Cookies may be used by our third-party contractors or our advertising partners to build a profile of your interests and show you relevant advertisements on other sites. We may share information about your use of our site with our social media, advertising, and analytics partners who may combine it with other information that you have provided to them or that they have collected from your use of their services. If you set your browser to block or delete Cookies, you will still see advertisements, but they will be less targeted to your interests.

The **University of Illinois System** is a [system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_system "University system") of [public universities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_universities "Public universities") in the U.S. state of [Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illinois "Illinois"), consisting of three campuses located in [Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago "University of Illinois Chicago"), [Springfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Springfield "University of Illinois Springfield"), and [Urbana-Champaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Urbana-Champaign "University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign"). Across all campuses, the University of Illinois System enrolls more than 101,000 students.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_System#cite_note-4) It had an operating budget of $7.18 billion in 2021.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_System#cite_note-about-5) Its oldest university, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, was established as the state's [land grant university](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land-grant_university "Land-grant university") in 1867.

## Organization

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Illinois_System&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Organization")]

See also: [List of presidents of the University of Illinois System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_presidents_of_the_University_of_Illinois_System "List of presidents of the University of Illinois System")

The University of Illinois System consists of three campuses in [Illinois Urbana-Champaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Urbana-Champaign "University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign"), [Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago "University of Illinois Chicago"), and [Springfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Springfield "University of Illinois Springfield"). The university in Urbana-Champaign is known as "Illinois", "U of I", or "UIUC", whereas the Chicago campus is known as "UIC" and the Springfield campus as "UIS".

The system is governed by a board of trustees consisting of thirteen members: the governor of Illinois serves as an [ex officio member](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ex_officio_member "Ex officio member"), nine trustees are appointed by the [governor of Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_of_Illinois "Governor of Illinois"), and a student trustee elected by referendum represents each of the system's three universities. One of the three student trustees is designated by the governor to have a vote.

The U of I System is led by the president, an executive vice president, a CFO/vice president of finance, a vice president for economic development and innovation, and the chancellors that lead each of the three universities. System leadership works to develop strategies and solutions to address educational and administrative challenges across the system. Centralized system offices staff support the work of the three universities by providing critical services that are vital to its missions.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_System#cite_note-6)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

The **Coalition of Urban Serving Universities** (commonly referred to as **USU**) is a selective organization of 39 U.S. public research universities located in [metropolitan areas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_area "Metropolitan area"). The USU member schools began formally meeting in 2005.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coalition_of_Urban_Serving_Universities#cite_note-members-1)

## Governance

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Coalition_of_Urban_Serving_Universities&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Governance")]

The USU Board of Directors is composed of Presidents and Chancellors of 10 member institutions. USU is headquartered in [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C.")[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coalition_of_Urban_Serving_Universities#cite_note-2)

The coalition has four specific areas of focus with the goal of strengthening communities throughout the nation via health and [community-involvement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Community_engagement "Community engagement") initiatives:[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coalition_of_Urban_Serving_Universities#cite_note-3)

*   The Education Pipeline/Urban Educator Corps - to improve the quality and quantity of urban teachers and implement evidence-based “cradle-to-career” education partnerships.
*   The Urban Health Initiative - to increase the number, diversity, and competence of the health workforce and reduce [health disparities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Health_disparities "Health disparities") in urban communities.
*   The Strengthening Communities Initiative - to revitalize neighborhoods, build community capacity, and strengthen regional economies.
*   Student Performance - Fostering Student Achievement to identify, assess with appropriate metrics, and disseminate substantive, scalable best practices along the continuum of efforts that support student success and degree completion.

**Marie Lynn Miranda** (born 1963) is an American economist, [data scientist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_scientist "Data scientist"), and academic administrator. She became the tenth chancellor of the [University of Illinois Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago "University of Illinois Chicago") and a vice president of the [University of Illinois System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_System "University of Illinois System") in July 2023. She previously served as provost and professor of applied [computational mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computational_mathematics "Computational mathematics") and statistics at the [University of Notre Dame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Notre_Dame "University of Notre Dame"). A self-taught [toxicologist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toxicologist "Toxicologist") and [environmental scientist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Environmental_scientist "Environmental scientist"), Miranda researches [children's environmental health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pediatric_environmental_health "Pediatric environmental health") and geospatial [health informatics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Health_informatics "Health informatics"). Her research through the Children's Environmental Health Initiative has informed [CDC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centers_for_Disease_Control_and_Prevention "Centers for Disease Control and Prevention") and [EPA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Environmental_Protection_Agency "United States Environmental Protection Agency") policy on childhood lead exposure. She is a Fellow of the American Association for the Advancement of Science and was recognized as a 2023 Woman of Note by Crain's Chicago Business.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Lynn_Miranda#cite_note-AAAS-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Lynn_Miranda#cite_note-Crain's_Chicago_Business-2)

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Marie_Lynn_Miranda&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Miranda was born in 1963.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Lynn_Miranda#cite_note-Mabry_2022-3) She is the first member of her family to be born in the United States.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Lynn_Miranda#cite_note-Fosmoe_2021-4) In 1961, her parents and three brothers moved to [South Bend, Indiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Bend,_Indiana "South Bend, Indiana") from [Goa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goa "Goa") while her father, Constancio Miranda, was studying civil engineering.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Lynn_Miranda#cite_note-Fosmoe_2021-4) He was later a professor at the [University of Detroit Mercy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Detroit_Mercy "University of Detroit Mercy").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Lynn_Miranda#cite_note-Sturdivant_2015-5) She attended Catholic schools in [Detroit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Detroit "Detroit").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Lynn_Miranda#cite_note-Fosmoe_2021-4) Miranda earned an A.B. in mathematics and economics, _[summa cum laude](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin\_honors "Latin honors")_, from [Duke University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_University "Duke University") in 1985.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Lynn_Miranda#cite_note-UICbio-6)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Lynn_Miranda#cite_note-Sturdivant_2015-5) She was inducted into [Phi Beta Kappa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phi_Beta_Kappa "Phi Beta Kappa") at Duke University.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Lynn_Miranda#cite_note-UICbio-6) She was also named a Truman Scholar.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Lynn_Miranda#cite_note-UICbio-6) While attending Duke University, she worked as a student manager for the [Duke Blue Devils men's basketball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_Blue_Devils_men's_basketball "Duke Blue Devils men's basketball") under coach [Mike Krzyzewski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Krzyzewski "Mike Krzyzewski").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Lynn_Miranda#cite_note-Fosmoe_2021-4) Miranda earned an M.A. (1988) and a Ph.D. in economics from [Harvard University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_University "Harvard University"), where she held a National Science Foundation Graduate Research Fellowship.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Lynn_Miranda#cite_note-UICbio-6)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Lynn_Miranda#cite_note-Sturdivant_2015-5) Her 1990 dissertation was titled, _Essays on Land Management_.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Lynn_Miranda#cite_note-Miranda_1990-7) Peter Timmer, Lawrence Goulder, and [Jerry Green](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerry_Green_(economist) "Jerry Green (economist)") served on her doctoral committee.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Lynn_Miranda#cite_note-Miranda_1990-7)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Marie_Lynn_Miranda&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

Miranda joined the faculty at Duke University in 1990.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Lynn_Miranda#cite_note-Sturdivant_2015-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Lynn_Miranda#cite_note-UICbio-6) She is a self-taught [toxicologist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toxicologist "Toxicologist") and environmental scientist and joined Duke's integrated toxicology and environmental health program in 1999.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Lynn_Miranda#cite_note-Sturdivant_2015-5)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Lynn_Miranda#cite_note-Petersen_2020-8) Miranda was the founding director of the [Children's Environmental Health Initiative](https://cehi.uic.edu/) (CEHI).[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Lynn_Miranda#cite_note-Sturdivant_2015-5) For nine years, she was the director of undergraduate programs for the [Nicholas School of the Environment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicholas_School_of_the_Environment "Nicholas School of the Environment").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Lynn_Miranda#cite_note-UICbio-6) As a data scientist, her research focuses on geospatial health informatics.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Lynn_Miranda#cite_note-Passle_2015-9)

From 2012 to 2015, Miranda was the Samuel A. Graham dean of the school of natural resources and environment at [University of Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Michigan "University of Michigan").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Lynn_Miranda#cite_note-10)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Lynn_Miranda#cite_note-UICbio-6) With a [quantitative methods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantitative_research "Quantitative research") background, she was a professor of pediatrics and [obstetrics and gynaecology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obstetrics_and_gynaecology "Obstetrics and gynaecology") at [Michigan Medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Medicine "Michigan Medicine").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Lynn_Miranda#cite_note-11)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Lynn_Miranda#cite_note-Passle_2015-9)

Miranda was the Howard R. Hughes Provost and a professor of statistics at [Rice University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rice_University "Rice University") from 2015 to 2019.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Lynn_Miranda#cite_note-Sturdivant_2015-5)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Lynn_Miranda#cite_note-Petersen_2020-8) As provost, she led the university's academic, research, scholarly, and creative programs with a $700 million annual operating budget.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Lynn_Miranda#cite_note-12) She also directed the planning and implementation of $230 million in strategic investments.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Lynn_Miranda#cite_note-13) When Hurricane Harvey struck Houston in August 2017, Miranda led the university's initial emergency response and later established the Hurricane Harvey Registry to track the storm's long-term health and housing impacts on the greater Houston community.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Lynn_Miranda#cite_note-14)

# University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign

The University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign upholds its land-grant heritage by pioneering education and public research to address today’s challenges. With 16 schools and colleges, including more than 150 undergraduate programs and more than 100 graduate and professional fields of study, the university is committed to innovation and societal impact to shape a brighter future in Illinois and globally.

Total enrollment _61,000+_

Undergraduates from Illinois _72%  
  
 (27,919)_

Degrees awarded annually _17,800+_

## Program Highlights

### Gies College of Business

[Gies College of Business](https://giesbusiness.illinois.edu/) is one of the nation's top 10 public undergraduate business schools. The school’s online MBA ([iMBA](https://giesonline.illinois.edu/explore-programs/online-mba)) program offers unparalleled flexibility and affordability, with highly engaging courses taught by top UIUC faculty.

### Grainger College of Engineering

The [Grainger College of Engineering](https://grainger.illinois.edu/) stands among the global leaders in engineering education, research, innovation, entrepreneurship, and societal impact with 41 top-ranked programs.

### College of Agricultural, Consumer and Environmental Sciences

The [College of Agricultural, Consumer and Environmental Sciences](https://aces.illinois.edu/) operates state-of-the-art labs and facilities, including UIUC’s Sustainable Student Farm. This gives students the hands-on experience necessary for global agriculture demands.

![Image 4: The Fighting Illini football team are honored on the basketball court at State Farm Center.](https://uillinois.edu/userfiles/servers/server_1240/image/illini20athletics201920x800.png)

## Athletics

The University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign competes in NCAA Division I sports and is a charter member of the Big Ten Conference and the NCAA. Fighting Illini teams have won 18 NCAA Championships, five football national championships, advanced to five NCAA Men's Basketball Final Fours, and won 248 Big Ten titles overall, the second-most in conference history.

[FightingIllini.com](https://fightingillini.com/)

## Featured Initiatives

### Leadership Labs

[Leadership Labs](https://leadership.illinois.edu/programs/leadership-labs) offer multi-hour seminars online, hybrid, and in person to nurture integrity and develop problem-solving skills for future roles.

### Chancellor's Call to Action Initiative

The [Chancellor's Call to Action Initiative](https://calltoaction.illinois.edu/) prioritizes the university’s core values of diversity, equity, and inclusion. Central to this dedication is a $2 million research endeavor aimed at furthering comprehension of systemic bias and structural disparities while developing innovative solutions.

### Chancellor for Arts Integration at Illinois

The [Chancellor for Arts Integration at Illinois](https://news.illinois.edu/view/6367/1147903170) focuses on interdisciplinary collaboration, connecting artists and social scientists on campus.

## Visit Our Reading Rooms

Copy link

 Special Collections and University Archives has two locations on the University of Illinois Chicago campus. Each location holds unique materials, contacting staff prior to visiting will help determine which location will be best for your research needs.   
  
 If you are visiting in person, please **[book an appointment](http://uic.libwizard.com/f/SCUAregistration)** at least two business days in advance of your visit. You are welcome to reserve time on multiple days if capacity allows. Unfortunately, same-day appointments or walk-ins cannot be accommodated at this time. 

*   Richard J. Daley Library

Located on the 3rd floor of the Richard J. Daley Library, this location holds archival collections and rare books, as well university records and faculty/staff papers related to the east side of campus.

Hours: Appointment only

801 S. Morgan St.  
 Chicago, IL 60607

Phone: (312) 996-2742 
*   Library of the Health Sciences - Chicago

Located on the 3rd floor of the Library of the Health Sciences-Chicago, this location holds archival collections and rare books focused on the history of the health sciences, as well university records and faculty/staff papers related to the west side of campus.

Hours: Appointment only

1750 W. Polk St.  
 Chicago, IL 60612

Phone: (312) 996-8977

### Champaign-Urbana

Champaign-Urbana has been named among the top 10 college towns in the country and ranked a top city for recent graduates. Visitors and locals enjoy inspiring food, art, music, artisans, parks, markets and festivals. ### Krannert Art Museum

Discover Krannert Art Museum's diverse collection, vibrant exhibitions and engaging programs. As the second-largest fine art museum in the state, the museum features over 11,000 artworks and a strong connection between the university and its community. [Visit Krannert Art Museum](https://kam.illinois.edu/)[Show Krannert Art Museum on the map](https://maps.app.goo.gl/QKYPgrHeuAmL5cN7A)  ![Image 33](https://illinois.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/KAM-6-1-1024x400.jpg) ![Image 34](https://illinois.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/KAM-8-1.jpg) ![Image 35](https://illinois.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/KAM-7-1.jpg) ![Image 36](https://illinois.edu/)

### Spurlock Museum

The Spurlock Museum of World Cultures, a regional hub for global cultural and archaeological collections, offers something for everyone — performances, lectures and visits. Its nine permanent exhibits showcase historical and contemporary cultures from around the world, while special exhibitions spark unique programs and events. Krannert Center for the Performing Arts, one of the nation's top university performance venues, spans seven acres with four theaters and an outdoor amphitheater. The University Library is one of the largest library collections in the country. It has approximately 30 subject libraries, area studies centers and special collections across campus and houses more than 15 million volumes and 24 million items. ### About Cookies

Cookies and related technologies (herein “Cookies”) are small text files that a website saves on your computer when you visit the site. Cookies the University sets are called first-party Cookies. The data collected might be about you, your device, your preferences, or your login information. Cookies set by third parties are called third-party Cookies. We use third-party Cookies for analyzing website traffic and our advertising and marketing efforts. Under each category heading below you will find a general description of the Cookies in each category. You can change your browser settings to block, delete, or alert you to Cookies. The Help menu on the menu bar of most browsers will tell you how to do that.  Strictly Necessary Cookies - Always Active 
Strictly Necessary Cookies are first-party Cookies that are necessary for the website to function. They can be either permanent or temporary and are usually only set in response to actions made directly by you that amount to a request for services, such as logging in or filling in forms. For example, we use Strictly Necessary Cookies to handle user registration and login. Some sites require the use of Strictly Necessary Cookies to access the site, such as University websites requiring University credentialed authentication. If you set your browser to block or delete Cookies, you may not be able to access the site or some parts of the site will not work.

 Performance Cookies - Always Active 
Performance Cookies allow us to count visits and traffic sources so we can measure and improve the performance and effectiveness of University websites. Performance Cookies also help the University understand which webpages are the most and least popular, see how visitors move around the site, and determine whether webpage content is relevant to user interests. Performance Cookies may be first-party or third party, permanent or temporary, and do not personally identify individual visitors. Some Performance Cookies are “analytics” Cookies (e.g., Google Analytics), using third-party software tools, which help us understand more about how our websites are used and where visitors come from by collecting and aggregating anonymous information on the pages visited and any advertisements viewed. The University does not take responsibility for the collection, use, and management of data by any third-party software tool provider unless required to do so by applicable law. If you set your browser to block or delete Cookies, some site services and functionalities may not work.

 Functional Cookies - Always Active 
Functional Cookies enhance the performance and functionality of our websites but are non-essential to their use. These permanent Cookies allow our website to remember information from your previous visits, such as details you submitted before or your previously stated preferences. These Cookies may also be used to provide services you request, such as newsletters or publications. They may be first- or third-party Cookies that enable services we have added to our webpages. If you set your browser to block or delete Cookies, some or all of these services may not function properly.

 Targeting Cookies - Always Active 
Targeting Cookies are used to deliver content tailored to your interests and may be temporary or permanent. They may also be first-party or third-party Cookies. Targeting Cookies are based on uniquely identifying your browser and device; they do not store information such as your name. December 26, 2017

The closing of 4-year-old Indiana Tech Law School in Fort Wayne, and the revelation that 138-year-old Valparaiso University Law School faced an uncertain future, made law school troubles the top legal news story of 2017, as determined by the staff of Indiana Lawyer. Changes on the federal and state bench also were among the year’s top stories.

[Read More](https://www.theindianalawyer.com/articles/45718-top-10-legal-stories-of-2017-focus-on-law-schools-courts-changes)

December 12, 2017

With the closing of Indiana Tech School of Law and an uncertain future for Valparaiso University School of Law, experts say there are no easy answers for the pressures facing legal education.

[Read More](https://www.theindianalawyer.com/articles/45600-legal-community-seeks-answers-for-law-schools-woes)

## [ABA withdrawing approval for Indiana Tech Law School](https://www.theindianalawyer.com/articles/45229-aba-withdrawing-approval-for-indiana-tech-law-school)

October 27, 2017

Roughly four months after Indiana Tech closed its law school, the American Bar Association is poised to withdraw provisional accreditation of the legal education program.

[Read More](https://www.theindianalawyer.com/articles/45229-aba-withdrawing-approval-for-indiana-tech-law-school)

## [Bar exam blues continue as July rate holds steady](https://www.theindianalawyer.com/articles/44995-bar-exam-blues-continue-as-july-rate-holds-steady)

October 3, 2017

Chief Justice Loretta Rush said she was worried and concerned about slumping bar exam scores. She echoed the apprehension of many about the quality of students being admitted to law schools and she noted the format of the test itself may be impacting the results.

[Read More](https://www.theindianalawyer.com/articles/44995-bar-exam-blues-continue-as-july-rate-holds-steady)

## [Indiana Tech disperses books from law library](https://www.theindianalawyer.com/articles/44225-indiana-tech-disperses-books-from-law-library)

July 11, 2017

A bulk of the books from the law library at the defunct Indiana Tech Law School are finding a new home at Ivy Tech Community College in Fort Wayne, while other volumes are going elsewhere.

[Read More](https://www.theindianalawyer.com/articles/44225-indiana-tech-disperses-books-from-law-library)

## [Top students still not interested in a JD](https://www.theindianalawyer.com/articles/44033-top-students-still-not-interested-in-a-law-degree)

June 19, 2017

A few months before law schools around the country begin a new academic year, the number of people applying for admission has slipped, with the greatest decline coming from applicants posting the highest LSAT scores.

[Read More](https://www.theindianalawyer.com/articles/44033-top-students-still-not-interested-in-a-law-degree)

May 26, 2017

As the law school’s last class graduates, its website has been taken down andstudents begin to transfer to other programs.

[Read More](https://www.theindianalawyer.com/articles/43828-indiana-techs-closing-of-law-school-leaves-unanswered-questions)

## [Last class graduates from Indiana Tech Law School](https://www.theindianalawyer.com/articles/43693-last-class-graduates-from-indiana-tech-law-school)

May 15, 2017

Waiting for graduation ceremonies to begin Saturday morning, Philip Davis summed up his place in the university’s history — at age 60, he is the oldest student who has ever graduated and ever will graduate from Indiana Tech Law School.

[Read More](https://www.theindianalawyer.com/articles/43693-last-class-graduates-from-indiana-tech-law-school)

Although deans consistently disparage the annual rankings, the U.S. News & World Report’s 2018 Best Law Schools may have given Indiana University Robert H. McKinney School of Law reason to cheer.

From law school troubles to new court initiatives, take a look back at the top stories in Indiana Lawyer this year.

New information released from the American Bar Association underscores the differences between Indiana’s law schools.

While those who have studied trends in legal education differ on whether Indiana Tech will be one in a string of closures, they agree that the first priority must be the students.

Indiana Tech Law School's closure is the first time in the collective memory of the American Bar Association that a law school has closed without transferring its assets.

November 8, 2023 |[Tyler Fenwick](https://www.theindianalawyer.com/authors/tyler-fenwick)

Three years after Valparaiso University Law School closed its doors, attorneys in northwest Indiana say they’re already seeing the impact of losing what had been a reliable feeder of lawyers into the surrounding communities.

[Read More](https://www.theindianalawyer.com/articles/valpo-law-closure-already-being-felt-in-northwest-indiana-after-3-years-shortage-of-attorneys-only-getting-worse-in-region)

## [Valparaiso looking for new team name after dropping Crusaders](https://www.theindianalawyer.com/articles/valparaiso-looking-for-new-team-name-after-dropping-crusaders)

February 12, 2021 |[Associated Press](https://www.theindianalawyer.com/authors/associated-press) and [IL Staff](https://www.theindianalawyer.com/authors/il-staff)

Valparaiso University announced Thursday that is dropping the team name Crusaders, the school mascot and all logos associated with the term that it says has been embraced by hate groups.

[Read More](https://www.theindianalawyer.com/articles/valparaiso-looking-for-new-team-name-after-dropping-crusaders)

## [Longtime Valparaiso attorney, radio show host Satterlee dies at 82](https://www.theindianalawyer.com/articles/longtime-valparaiso-attorney-radio-show-host-satterlee-dies-at-82)

December 2, 2020 |[IL Staff](https://www.theindianalawyer.com/authors/il-staff)

A longtime attorney and managing partner of a Valparaiso law firm who also was an entrepreneur and known for co-hosting a weekly jazz radio program has died, his former firm announced Wednesday. William F. (Bill) Satterlee was 82.

Here are the most-read stories on our website for the calendar year and their original dates of publication.

**1. Indianapolis attorney suspended for charging, collecting unreasonable fee**_(Sept. 29)_

At the time of the alleged misconduct, Indianapolis attorney Zachary Kester served as the managing attorney for Indianapolis-based Charitable Allies Inc., which was marketed as a “nonprofit for nonprofits” that provides “low bono” legal services.

**2. Indiana Supreme Court disciplines Evansville attorney for allegedly failing to protect client’s interests**_(March 7)_

Evansville attorney Brian Oberst was suspended for 90 days for allegedly failing to protect the interests of a client he was representing in a property dispute case.

**3. Attorney disbarred for sexual relations with three ‘vulnerable’ clients**_(Feb. 17)_

The Indiana Supreme Court said Winamac attorney Nathan Pearson was disbarred because his actions were predatory, not just merely exercises in poor judgment.

**4. Hendricks County brothers named in dozens of lawsuits over real estate deals**_(March 17)_

Jeremy Tucker was named as a defendant or co-defendant in more than 25 cases in Hamilton, Hendricks, Marion and Shelby counties. Joshua Tucker was named as a defendant or co-defendant in 18 local cases—including some of the cases in which Jeremy Tucker is named.

**5. Howard County judge permanently banned from judicial service**_(Sept. 12)_

Howard Superior Court Judge Matthew J. Elkin was banned from the bench for failing to maintain ethical boundaries and making injudicious statements in court.

**6. Indy attorney indefinitely suspended for noncooperation with the disciplinary commission**_(Dec. 9)_

Attorney John Hurley was moved to an indefinite suspension after the Indiana Supreme Court found that more than 90 days had passed since Hurley was initially suspended for failing to cooperate with the disciplinary process.

**7. Federal magistrate in Indy calls for discipline against attorney who used false AI citations**_(March 20)_

A federal magistrate judge in Indianapolis called for attorney Rafael Ramirez of Rio Hondo, Texas, to pay $15,000 and be considered for further discipline after he submitted briefs containing citations to non-existent cases that were obtained using artificial intelligence.

**8. Indiana attorney Zuckerberg sues Meta over accusations he’s impersonating Facebook founder**_(Sept. 2)_

Indianapolis bankruptcy attorney Mark Zuckerberg filed a lawsuit against Facebook’s parent company Meta, accusing it of negligence and breach of contract for continuously deactivating or suspending his social media accounts for unjust and improper reasons.

**9. Fort Wayne becomes latest target of Rokita’s expanding immigration-related inquiry**_(Dec. 17)_

The move into Fort Wayne came even as Indiana Attorney General Todd Rokita’s unconventional approach to the immigration probe had been successfully challenged in Evansville.

**10. Will there be more executions in Indiana in 2025?**_(Jan. 15)_

Indiana ended its 15-year pause on the execution of inmates sentenced to death in December 2024. Many wondered if the high cost of the lethal-injection drug or re-energized opposition to the death penalty might cause the state to reconsider the resumption. The answer came with two more executions as 2025 unfolded.•

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Leader of a university or college

A **chancellor** is a leader of a [college](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College "College") or [university](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University "University"), usually either the executive or ceremonial head of a university or of a campus within a [university system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_system "University system").

In most [Commonwealth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_of_Nations "Commonwealth of Nations") and former Commonwealth nations, the chancellor is usually a ceremonial non-resident head of the university. In such institutions, the chief executive of a university is the vice-chancellor, who may carry an additional title such as "[president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_president "University president")" (e.g., "president and vice-chancellor"). The chancellor may serve as chairperson of the governing body; otherwise, this duty is held by a chairperson who may be known as a [pro-chancellor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pro-chancellor "Pro-chancellor").

In many countries, the administrative and educational head of the university is known as the president, [principal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principal_(academia) "Principal (academia)") or [rector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rector_(academia) "Rector (academia)"). In the United States, the head of a university is usually referred to as the university president, while the executive head of a specific campus within a multi-campus university system may have the title of chancellor and report to the overall system's president, although the titles are sometimes reversed.

## Chancellor

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chancellor_(education)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Chancellor")]

### Australia and New Zealand

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chancellor_(education)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Australia and New Zealand")]

[![Image 4: icon](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/9/99/Question_book-new.svg/60px-Question_book-new.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Question_book-new.svg)This section **does not [cite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citing_sources "Wikipedia:Citing sources") any [sources](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability "Wikipedia:Verifiability")**. Please help [improve this section](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:EditPage/Chancellor_(education) "Special:EditPage/Chancellor (education)") by [adding citations to reliable sources](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Referencing_for_beginners "Help:Referencing for beginners"). Unsourced material may be challenged and [removed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability#Burden_of_evidence "Wikipedia:Verifiability")._(August 2025)_ _([Learn how and when to remove this message](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Maintenance\_template\_removal "Help:Maintenance template removal"))_

In both Australia and New Zealand, a chancellor is the chairperson of a university's governing body; thus, as well as having ceremonial duties, the chancellor participates in the governance of the university (but not its active management). The chancellor is assisted by a deputy chancellor (known as the pro-chancellor in some universities). The chancellor and deputy chancellor are frequently drawn from the senior ranks of business or the judiciary (it is one of the few jobs considered compatible with judicial service). Some universities have a visitor who is senior to the chancellor. University disputes can be appealed from the governing board to the visitor (as is still the case in the UK), but nowadays, such appeals are generally prohibited by legislation, and the position has only ceremonial functions (unlike the chancellor and deputy chancellor, who frequently preside at functions such as graduations, the visitor rarely attends university functions). The vice-chancellor usually serves as the chief executive of the university.

[Macquarie University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macquarie_University "Macquarie University") in Sydney is an anomaly as it once had the unique position of Emeritus Deputy Chancellor, a post created for [John Lincoln](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Lincoln_(judge) "John Lincoln (judge)") upon his retirement from his long-held post of deputy chancellor in 2000. The position was not merely an honorary title, as it also retained for Lincoln a place in the University Council until his death in 2011.

### Bangladesh

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chancellor_(education)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Bangladesh")]

The chancellor is a titular position in Bangladesh and is always held by the incumbent President of Bangladesh under the Private Universities Act 1992.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chancellor_(education)#cite_note-act-1) The position in public universities is not fixed for the president under any acts or laws (since the erection of a state university in Bangladesh requires an act to be passed in itself),[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chancellor_(education)#cite_note-moe-2) but it has been the custom so far to name the incumbent president of the country as chancellor of all state universities thus established. The day-to-day operations of the university are run by the vice-chancellor. The vice-chancellor has a deputy called the pro-vice-chancellor.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

## About us

Since 1990, The Indiana Lawyer has kept a finger on the pulse of Indiana’s legal community and reports on the issues that matter to you. We cover news from the courts, bar associations, law firms, legal aid, law schools, state government and more. Our daily newsletter keeps you up to date on the most recent court opinions from Indiana's appellate courts, as well as legal news happening in the state and nationally. Sign up for the free email at https://www.theindianalawyer.com/registration. You can also sign up for our Breaking News and News Updates at that link. We also bring you the latest in legal news via our The Indiana Lawyer Podcast. Get it on our website, in our free email or on your favorite podcast app. We're also committed to community engagement. Each year, we honor the legal community's outstanding lawyers and legal support staffers through our Leadership in Law Awards, which began in 2006. And in 2023, we began recognizing leaders in DEI efforts through our Diversity in Law Awards. Visit http://www.theindianalawyer.com for more information and to subscribe.
